headline: UK introduces 'Cutting Costs' Bill to put EU food and carbon-market deals into law

terms.meaning: A deal on sanitary and phytosanitary rules, the health checks on food, animals and plants traded between countries.
A scheme that puts a price on carbon pollution so that firms pay for what they emit.

levels.headline: UK introduces 'Cutting Costs' Bill to put EU food and carbon-market deals into law
levels.body:
The government introduced the 'Cutting Costs' (European Partnership) Bill in the House of Commons on 26 November. It would write two UK-EU agreements into UK law: a food and drink deal, known as the Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) agreement, and a deal linking the UK and EU carbon markets under their Emissions Trading Systems.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed the package at the UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November. Ministers say it is worth up to £17 billion a year, and could add up to 0.5% to UK GDP by 2040.
Government material says it would end the need for Export Health Certificates costing up to £200 each, remove 'Not for EU' labels from most products and replace single-use animal health certificates with multi-use pet passports. About £6.5 billion of British exports, including steel and aluminium, would be exempt from the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
Euronews reports that MPs are due to debate the Bill on 7 December. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has called the deal a betrayal of Brexit.
levels.why: It is the first step in turning the Brussels summit deal into law, and it will test whether the Commons backs closer ties with the EU.

MPs are due to debate the Bill on 7 December, according to Euronews. Nigel Farage of Reform UK says the deal betrays Brexit.
levels.why: It shows how far the government is going in rebuilding trade links with the EU, and how contested that is.

levels.headline: Bill to turn UK-EU food and carbon deals into law reaches the Commons

levels.why: The Bill decides whether the summit promises become real changes for businesses and shoppers.

levels.headline: New Bill would make trading with the EU cheaper and easier
levels.body:
The government has introduced a new law, called the 'Cutting Costs' Bill, in Parliament. It would put two deals with the European Union into UK law. One covers food and drink. The other links the UK and EU systems for charging firms for carbon pollution.

levels.why: It could mean cheaper, simpler trade with our nearest neighbours, but not everyone agrees it is a good idea.

levels.headline: A new law would make selling food to Europe cheaper

levels.headline: A new law could make it easier to sell food to Europe

levels.headline: The government wants to make selling things to Europe easier

levels.headline: A new rule could make it easier to sell food to Europe
levels.body:

This week the government asked MPs to agree to a new rule. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, made a deal with Europe on 20 November. The new rule would stop many of those forms. That could save firms a lot of money, up to £17 billion every year.

levels.headline: Britain and Europe agree to make sharing food easier
levels.body:
Think about swapping snacks at school. It is easier if there are no strict rules about what you can swap. Countries can be a bit like that too.
Britain and the countries of Europe have agreed to make it easier to send food to each other. They made the deal on 20 November. Now the government wants a new law to make it official, and the grown-ups in Parliament will talk about it on 7 December.
The deal could mean less paperwork for people who make and sell food. It could also mean a pet cat or dog gets a passport that works many times. The government thinks this could save a lot of money. Some grown-ups think it is a good idea and some do not.
levels.why: When countries get along and share more easily, it can help families in many ways.

headline: UK-EU food deal carries exit penalty, legal text shows, as Reform and Conservatives eye unpicking it

levels.headline: UK-EU food deal carries exit penalty, legal text shows, as Reform and Conservatives eye unpicking it
levels.body:
Legal text of the UK-EU food and drink agreement shows that a side leaving the deal early would have to pay. Euronews reports that the termination clause would require the party that exits to cover 'reasonable and proportionate costs' of restoring the infrastructure that the agreement removes.
The clause matters because the deal is likely to be politically contested. Reform UK and the Conservatives have both signalled that they would consider unpicking Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Brexit reset if they win power at the next general election, which is due in 2029.
The agreement is one of two that the government is turning into law through the 'Cutting Costs' (European Partnership) Bill, introduced in the Commons on 26 November. Ministers say the package could be worth up to £17 billion a year.
The cost of leaving, which the text leaves to be judged as reasonable and proportionate, could shape how easy it would be for a future government to reverse the deal.
levels.why: The exit cost could make it harder and more expensive for a future government to undo the deal.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closed down 0.25% at 7,182.78 in its last completed session on Wednesday, as US markets pause for Thanksgiving
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Wednesday 25 November, the last completed trading session. It slipped 0.25% to 7,182.78. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.33%, or 164.25 points, to 50,182.95, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% to 23,585.80, according to CNBC.
The Dow had been down by more than 1,100 points at its low, before a rebound. US markets were closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving, and Friday's session is shortened, closing at 1pm Eastern time. At the time of writing it had not yet opened.
The week has followed a sharp sell-off driven by worries about artificial intelligence shares. Futures pointed to a higher open on Friday, with S&P 500 futures up about 1.7%.
Traders also expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its December meeting: CME's FedWatch tool put the chance of a quarter-point rise at 98%.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions and savings, and rate-hike expectations affect the cost of borrowing.

headline: EU leaders fail to agree seven-year budget as Costa cuts summit short and talks move to 17 December

terms.meaning: The EU's spending plan for several years, here the next seven-year budget.
Money that EU countries borrow together, with all of them responsible for paying it back.

levels.headline: EU leaders fail to agree seven-year budget as Costa cuts summit short and talks move to 17 December
levels.body:
A special European Council summit on the EU's next seven-year budget ended without a deal. European Council President Antonio Costa cut the summit short, having planned for it to last two days, and Euronews described the talks as ending in disarray as leaders held on to their red lines. The so-called frugal countries walked out of group talks.
Negotiations are due to restart at the next EU summit on 17 December. France has warned that they cannot run beyond the end of the year because of its presidential election next spring, and Macron has threatened to end the talks if there is no deal in December.
The budget is tied to support for Ukraine. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said the two are directly linked. Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia and Bulgaria have said they will not take part in any future joint debt.
levels.why: The budget decides how EU money is spent for years, including help for Ukraine, and the clock is running down.

headline: Eurozone leaders back Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde as ECB president

terms.meaning: The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the 21 countries that use the euro.

levels.headline: Eurozone leaders back Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde as ECB president
levels.body:
A majority of eurozone leaders have backed Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos to become the next president of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde, Euronews and CNBC report. He won the support ahead of Klaas Knot, the former Dutch central bank governor.
The appointment is not yet final. The European Council is expected to make it in December, after consulting the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, neither of which has a veto. Lagarde announced on 29 October that she will step down on 7 February 2027, almost nine months before her term ends.
Hernández de Cos, who was governor of the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024 and has run the Bank for International Settlements since July 2025, would be the first Spaniard to lead the ECB. He would take over as euro area inflation stands at 4% for October, its highest in more than three years. Analysts see him as a pragmatic centrist.
levels.why: The ECB president sets the course for interest rates and prices across the euro area.

levels.headline: Eurozone leaders back Hernández de Cos as next ECB president

levels.why: Who runs the ECB matters for borrowing costs and prices in the 21 euro countries.

levels.why: The next ECB boss will have to deal with high inflation.

levels.headline: Most eurozone leaders back a Spanish economist to run the European Central Bank

headline: Brent crude near $96, close to its highest this month, as Hormuz and Saudi attacks outweigh surplus fears

terms.meaning: The main international price benchmark for oil.
A group of oil-producing countries that agree how much oil to pump.

levels.headline: Brent crude near $96, close to its highest this month, as Hormuz and Saudi attacks outweigh surplus fears
levels.body:
Brent crude traded around $96 a barrel on Friday morning, close to its highest level this month. Brent futures were down 38 cents at $96.19 by 0140 GMT, after gaining nearly $2 on Thursday to settle at their highest since 6 November, CNBC reported. On Wednesday Brent had risen 3.5% to settle at $94.61.
The rise reflects attacks in the Middle East. Iran has continued to strike ships in the Strait of Hormuz, and Yemen's Houthis have targeted Saudi energy sites. The International Energy Agency expects the oil market to return to a surplus in the fourth quarter, and prices remain well below the October highs, when Brent traded near $116.
OPEC+ ministers meet on 29 November to decide output policy for 2027. Analysts disagree on direction: ANZ thinks Brent could rise above $100, while Eurasia Group expects it to stay in the lower half of an $80 to $100 range.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and shop prices, and so into inflation.

levels.headline: Brent crude edges towards $96 as Middle East attacks outweigh oversupply worries
levels.body:

levels.why: Higher oil prices can push up fuel and transport costs for households and firms.

headline: UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October as motor fuel pushed transport costs up 6.6%, ahead of a possible December rate rise

terms.meaning: The Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of how fast the prices of everyday goods and services are rising.
The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences mortgage and savings rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October as motor fuel pushed transport costs up 6.6%, ahead of a possible December rate rise
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.6% in the year to October from 3.5% in September, according to ONS figures published on 18 November and reported by Trading Economics. Transport inflation climbed to 6.6% from 4.6%, driven mainly by motor fuels. The ONS's CPIH measure, which includes housing costs, stood at 3.7%.
The pressure comes from higher energy prices linked to the conflict involving Iran. The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by a quarter of a point to 4% on 5 November, its first rise since 2023, by eight votes to one, and said it expects inflation to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027.
Analysts quoted by CNBC say recent economic figures keep a further rise in December firmly on the table, and markets had priced about a one-in-four chance of one after the November decision. Oil near $96 a barrel adds to the risk that fuel costs stay high.
levels.why: Rising prices squeeze household budgets and can mean more expensive mortgages if rates rise again.

levels.headline: UK inflation edges up to 3.6% in October as petrol and diesel costs lift transport prices

CNBC reports that analysts see a December rise as firmly on the table. With Brent crude near $96 a barrel, fuel costs may stay high.
levels.why: Higher inflation reduces what wages and savings can buy and keeps pressure on the Bank to raise rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.6% as fuel costs push up the price of getting around

Energy prices are being pushed up by the conflict involving Iran. The Bank of England raised its main interest rate to 4% on 5 November, its first increase since 2023, and expects inflation to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027.
Some analysts say another rise in December is possible. Brent crude is near $96 a barrel, so fuel could stay expensive.
levels.why: Higher prices and possible higher interest rates both hit household budgets.

levels.why: It means everyday costs keep rising and borrowing could get dearer.

headline: CBI retail sales gauge improves to minus 10 in November from minus 55, but outlook stays fragile as shoppers stay cautious

terms.meaning: In a survey, the share of firms reporting rising sales minus the share reporting falling sales. A negative number means more firms saw falls.
The value of goods that shops sell to the public.

levels.headline: CBI retail sales gauge improves to minus 10 in November from minus 55, but outlook stays fragile as shoppers stay cautious
levels.body:
The CBI's retail sales balance improved to minus 10 in November from minus 55 in October, better than expected, according to Trading Economics. A negative balance means more retailers reported falling sales than rising ones, so the figure shows sales were still weaker overall, but far less so than a month earlier.
The CBI said the outlook remained fragile, pointing to cautious household spending and higher fuel costs. The latest ONS data are firmer, with official figures saying retail sales rose in the three months to October, and Trading Economics putting October's monthly rise at 0.7% and annual growth at 2.3%.
The picture sits alongside inflation of 3.6% in October and a Bank of England that raised interest rates to 4% on 5 November. Higher prices and borrowing costs both make shoppers more careful, which matters for the shops that rely on the run-up to Christmas.
levels.why: Shop sales show how confident households feel, just as the Christmas trading season gets under way.

levels.headline: CBI retail survey improves to minus 10 as shops see a smaller fall in sales, but caution remains
levels.body:
The CBI's retail sales balance rose to minus 10 in November from minus 55 in October, beating expectations, Trading Economics reports. A negative reading means more retailers reported falling sales than rising sales, so conditions are still weak but much less so than before.
The CBI said the outlook is still fragile because households are being careful with money and fuel costs are higher. Official ONS data are firmer: retail sales rose in the three months to October, and Trading Economics reports October's monthly gain at 0.7% with annual growth of 2.3%.
Inflation was 3.6% in October and the Bank of England raised rates to 4% on 5 November, both of which weigh on shoppers ahead of Christmas.
levels.why: It gives an early read on how well shops may do over Christmas.

levels.headline: Shops report fewer sales falls in November, but the CBI says the outlook is still fragile
levels.body:
A survey by the CBI shows retail conditions improved in November. Its retail sales balance rose to minus 10 from minus 55 in October, better than expected, Trading Economics reports. A balance below zero means more shops reported falling sales than rising sales.
The CBI said the outlook is still fragile because households are being cautious and fuel costs are higher. Official data from the Office for National Statistics are firmer, showing retail sales rose in the three months to October. Trading Economics puts October's monthly rise at 0.7% and annual growth at 2.3%.
Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October and the Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% on 5 November, which weigh on spending as Christmas approaches.
levels.why: It shows how confident shoppers are as the Christmas trading period begins.

levels.headline: Shops report a smaller fall in sales in November, CBI survey shows
levels.body:
A survey by the CBI, a business group, shows retail sales were less bad in November. Its balance improved to minus 10 from minus 55 in October, which was better than expected, Trading Economics reports. A minus figure means more shops saw sales fall than rise.
The CBI says the outlook is still fragile because shoppers are cautious and fuel costs are higher. Official figures look better. The Office for National Statistics says retail sales rose in the three months to October, and one data provider puts October's rise at 0.7% over the month.
Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October and the Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% in early November. That leaves less room in many family budgets just before Christmas.
levels.why: Shops depend on Christmas spending, so this shows how confident shoppers are.

levels.headline: Shop sales are still weak in November, but better than October
levels.body:
A business group called the CBI asks shops every month whether their sales are going up or down. Its score for November was minus 10, which is better than October's minus 55. Because it is below zero, more shops said their sales fell than said they rose. It was better than experts had guessed.
The CBI says things are still shaky because people are being careful with money and fuel costs more. Other figures from the Office for National Statistics are more positive. They say shop sales rose in the three months to October.
Prices are up 3.6% on a year ago, and interest rates are 4%. That leaves families with less to spend before Christmas.
levels.why: If shoppers hold back, shops may struggle at their busiest time of year.

levels.headline: Shops did a bit better in November, but people are still careful with money
levels.body:
A business group called the CBI asks shops if sales are going up or down. It gives a score. In November the score was minus 10. In October it was minus 55. A score below zero means more shops saw sales fall than rise. So November was still not good, but it was much better than October.
The CBI says things are still shaky. Families are being careful with their money, and petrol costs more. Official figures from the Office for National Statistics look better. They say shop sales went up in the three months to October.
Prices are about 3.6% higher than a year ago. Interest rates are 4%. Both make life a bit harder for families.
levels.why: Shops need families to spend at Christmas, so careful shoppers are bad news for them.

levels.headline: Shops had a better November, but families are still careful with money
levels.body:
A business group called the CBI asks shops every month whether sales are going up or down, and turns the answers into a score. In October the score was minus 55. In November it was minus 10. A score below zero means more shops said sales fell than said they rose, so things are still weak. But they are much better than before.
The CBI says things are still shaky. Families are being careful with money and fuel costs more. Some official figures are better. They say shops sold more in the three months to October.
Prices are up 3.6% on last year, and interest rates are 4%. That makes families think hard before spending, just before Christmas.
levels.why: Shops need families to spend, so careful spending is hard for them.

levels.headline: Shops had a better month, but people are still being careful
levels.body:
Every month, a business group called the CBI asks shops how their sales are going. It turns the answers into a score. In October the score was minus 55. In November it was minus 10. Minus means more shops said sales went down than up. So things got better, but they are still not great.
The CBI says people are still being careful with money, and petrol costs more. Some official figures look happier. They say shops sold more over the three months up to October.
Things cost more than a year ago, and borrowing money costs more too. That makes families think hard about what to buy, just before Christmas.
levels.why: Shops need people to spend, so careful families can make a hard time for them.

levels.headline: Shops did a little better this month, but people still count their pennies
levels.body:
Every month, a group asks shops if they sold more or less than before. It turns the answers into a score. In October, the score was very low, minus 55. In November, it was minus 10. That is still below zero, so more shops sold less than sold more. But it is much better.
The group says people are still careful with money. Petrol costs more, and so do lots of things in the shops. Families have to think hard before they buy.
Christmas is the busiest time of year for shops. They want lots of people to come and buy presents.
levels.why: Shops need customers, and customers need money to spend.

levels.headline: Shops sold a bit more this month, but people are still careful
levels.body:
Imagine you run a lemonade stall. Some weeks lots of people buy a cup. Some weeks hardly anyone does. Shops are like that too.
A group asked shops how they did in October. Most said they sold less than before. Then they asked again in November. This time, fewer shops said they sold less. So things got a bit better, but they are still not as good as shops would like.
People are being careful with their money, because lots of things cost more now. Christmas is coming, and shops hope families will come and buy presents.
levels.why: When families spend less, shops can have a hard time.

headline: Projectile hits Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery, killing a worker, as Iran claims more mine strikes in Hormuz

terms.meaning: An Iran-aligned armed group in Yemen.
A narrow sea passage at the mouth of the Gulf through which a large share of the world's oil travels.

levels.headline: Projectile hits Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery, killing a worker, as Iran claims more mine strikes in Hormuz
levels.body:
A projectile struck Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery on Thursday 26 November, temporarily halting some operations, killing a Nepalese worker and wounding several others, according to Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry. The report did not name who was responsible, though Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have claimed attacks on Saudi targets.
The day before, the Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery and Riyadh's financial district, and they have also claimed attacks on the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan.
Separately, Iranian forces reported that an oil tanker hit a naval mine and caught fire in a restricted zone of the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has said three tankers hit mines. Israel has said it is prepared to launch fresh strikes against Iran even without US military involvement.
The attacks have helped push Brent crude close to $96 a barrel.
levels.why: Attacks on oil sites and shipping threaten global energy supplies and keep prices high.

levels.headline: Saudi refinery hit by projectile as Houthis step up attacks and Iran reports tanker mine strikes
levels.body:
A projectile hit Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery on Thursday 26 November, temporarily stopping some operations. A Nepalese worker was killed and several people were wounded, according to Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry. It did not say who fired it, but Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have been claiming attacks on Saudi sites.
On Wednesday the Houthis said they had attacked the Ras Tanura refinery and Riyadh's financial district. They have also claimed attacks on the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan.
Iran meanwhile says tankers have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and reported a tanker on fire in a restricted zone. Israel has said it is ready to strike Iran again, even without US forces.
The violence has lifted oil prices, with Brent near $96 a barrel.
levels.why: The attacks raise the risk of wider conflict and higher energy costs for the world.

levels.headline: Worker killed after projectile hits Saudi refinery as tension grows around Hormuz
levels.body:
A projectile hit a Saudi Aramco refinery at Jazan on Thursday 26 November. Some operations stopped for a time, a Nepalese worker was killed and several others were hurt, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said. It did not say who was behind it. The Houthis, an armed group in Yemen linked to Iran, have claimed attacks on Saudi targets.
On Wednesday the Houthis said they hit the Ras Tanura refinery and Riyadh's financial district. They also claimed attacks on the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan.
Iran has said tankers have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, an important shipping route. Israel has said it is ready to strike Iran again even without help from the US.
Oil prices have risen, with Brent close to $96 a barrel.
levels.why: What happens in the Gulf affects the price of fuel around the world.

levels.headline: A worker is killed after an attack on a Saudi oil refinery
levels.body:
A projectile hit an oil refinery at Jazan in Saudi Arabia on Thursday 26 November. The refinery belongs to Saudi Aramco. Some work stopped for a while. A worker from Nepal was killed and several other people were hurt, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said. It did not say who did it. A group in Yemen called the Houthis, who are linked to Iran, say they have attacked Saudi sites.
On Wednesday the Houthis said they had hit a refinery at Ras Tanura and part of the city of Riyadh.
Iran says oil tankers have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route. Israel says it is ready to attack Iran again, even without US help.
Oil prices have gone up.
levels.why: The attacks put people at risk and could make oil and petrol more expensive.

levels.headline: Worker killed after a projectile hits a Saudi oil refinery, as Iran says ships hit mines
levels.body:
A projectile hit an oil refinery at Jazan in Saudi Arabia on Thursday 26 November. Some work stopped for a time. A worker from Nepal was killed and several people were hurt, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said. It did not say who was responsible. Yemen's Houthis, who are linked to Iran, have claimed attacks on Saudi sites, including the Ras Tanura refinery on Wednesday.
Iran says oil tankers have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route that carries a lot of the world's oil. Israel says it is ready to strike Iran again, even without US help.
Because of the fighting, oil prices have risen. Brent is near $96 a barrel.
levels.why: The attacks put workers at risk and could keep energy costs high around the world.

levels.headline: A worker has died after an attack on an oil site in Saudi Arabia
levels.body:
On Thursday 26 November, something flew into an oil refinery in Jazan, Saudi Arabia. The refinery belongs to a company called Saudi Aramco. Some of the work had to stop. A worker from Nepal died and several others were hurt, the Saudi government said. It did not say who did it.
A group in Yemen called the Houthis say they have attacked oil sites in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis are friends with Iran. On Wednesday they said they had hit another refinery.
Iran says oil ships have hit mines in a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. A mine is a bomb in the water. Israel says it is ready to attack Iran again. Oil prices have risen.
levels.why: Fighting in this region can make oil more expensive for all of us.

levels.headline: An oil site in Saudi Arabia is hit and a worker dies
levels.body:
On Thursday something hit an oil site in Saudi Arabia, called the Jazan refinery. A refinery is a factory that turns oil into fuel. Some of the work stopped. A worker from Nepal died and some other people were hurt. The Saudi government said so. It did not say who did it.
A group in Yemen, called the Houthis, says it has attacked oil sites in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis are friends with Iran, which is fighting with the US and Israel.
Iran also says some oil ships have hit mines in the sea, near a narrow sea road called the Strait of Hormuz. A mine is a hidden bomb in the water. Because of the fighting, oil costs more.
levels.why: When oil sites are attacked, oil can cost more and people can be hurt.

levels.headline: An oil factory in Saudi Arabia is hit, and a worker has died
levels.body:
On Thursday, something hit an oil factory in Saudi Arabia. The factory is called a refinery. It turns oil into fuel. Some work stopped. A man from Nepal who worked there died, and some other people were hurt. This is very sad.
The government of Saudi Arabia did not say who did it. A group in Yemen, called the Houthis, says it has attacked oil places in Saudi Arabia. Iran is friends with the Houthis. Iran is also in a fight with other countries.
Iran says some oil ships hit hidden bombs in the sea, near a narrow sea road called the Strait of Hormuz. Because of this fighting, oil costs more.
levels.why: Fighting can hurt workers and make fuel cost more.

levels.headline: Sad news from a Saudi oil factory
levels.body:
On Thursday, something flew into a big oil factory in Saudi Arabia. Oil is turned into fuel there. A worker from Nepal died and some others were hurt. That is very sad.
A group in Yemen says it has been attacking places in Saudi Arabia. Grown-ups are still working out what happened and who is to blame.
There is also trouble in the sea nearby. Some ships that carry oil hit hidden bombs in the water. Ships have to be very careful there.
When oil is hard to get, it costs more. That is why people around the world are watching the news closely.
levels.why: When there is fighting, people can get hurt, and the things we buy can cost more.

levels.headline: Trouble near some oil factories far away
levels.body:
Far away, in a country called Saudi Arabia, there are big factories that make fuel from oil. On Thursday something hit one of them. A worker died and some others were hurt. That is sad.
Some people in a nearby country say they have been attacking places in Saudi Arabia. There is also trouble at sea. Ships that carry oil have to sail along a narrow sea road, and some of them have hit hidden bombs.
When there is trouble like this, there can be less oil in the world. When something is harder to get, it costs more, like a toy that every child wants. Grown-ups are working hard to stop the fighting.
levels.why: Fighting far away can make fuel dearer at home, and it hurts real people.

headline: China's industrial profits surge 20.1% in October, the fastest since May, as regulators cut margin requirements

terms.meaning: The earnings of large manufacturers, mining firms and utilities, used as a gauge of factory-sector health.
Borrowing money from a broker to buy shares.

levels.headline: China's industrial profits surge 20.1% in October, the fastest since May, as regulators cut margin requirements
levels.body:
China's industrial profits grew 20.1% in October from a year earlier, the fastest pace since May, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. The figures were published on Friday 27 November.
Also on Friday, regulators moved to steady share markets after an AI-led sell-off across Asia. Exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing will cut the minimum margin ratio for margin-financed share purchases to 80% from 100% from 30 November, which lets investors borrow more to buy shares.
Asian shares recovered on Thursday after the sell-off. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16, though on 19 November it had fallen 5.06% in a day. Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose 1.52% in its last hour on Thursday, and mainland China's CSI 300 closed at 3,900.55.
Global shares rallied on Thursday, largely looking past new US tariffs announced by the White House.
levels.why: Factory profits show how healthy China's economy is, and Asian markets influence global investors.

levels.headline: China's industrial profits jump 20.1% in October as exchanges ease margin rules
levels.body:
Profits at China's industrial firms rose 20.1% in October compared with a year earlier, the fastest growth since May, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. The data were released on Friday 27 November.
On the same day, exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing said they would cut the minimum margin ratio for margin-financed share purchases to 80% from 100%, starting 30 November. That means investors can borrow more to buy shares, and comes as Asian regulators try to steady markets after an AI-led sell-off.
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 on Thursday after a 5.06% fall on 19 November. Hong Kong's Hang Seng gained 1.52% in its last hour on Thursday and the CSI 300 closed at 3,900.55.
Global shares rallied on Thursday, largely ignoring new US tariffs.
levels.why: Strong factory profits and looser rules may help calm nervous investors.

levels.headline: China's factory profits rise 20.1% as authorities act to steady shares
levels.body:
Profits at China's large industrial firms grew 20.1% in October compared with a year earlier. That is the fastest rate since May, the National Bureau of Statistics said on Friday 27 November.
The same day, share exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing announced a change aimed at supporting markets. From 30 November, the minimum margin ratio for margin-financed share purchases falls to 80% from 100%. In practice, this lets investors borrow more to buy shares. It follows a sell-off in AI-related shares across Asia.
Shares have since partly recovered. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 on Thursday, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose 1.52% in its last hour. Global shares also rallied on Thursday, despite new US tariffs announced by the White House.
levels.why: Chinese factory profits are a sign of demand for goods made around the world.

levels.headline: Profits at Chinese factories jump 20.1% in October
levels.body:
The profits of big Chinese factories, mines and power firms were 20.1% higher in October than a year earlier. That is the fastest rise since May, the National Bureau of Statistics said on Friday 27 November.
On the same day, the stock exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing said they will make it a bit easier to borrow money to buy shares. From 30 November, buyers will need to put down 80% of the cost instead of 100%. This follows a sharp fall in shares linked to artificial intelligence across Asia.
Shares have bounced back a little. Japan's Nikkei index rose 0.86% on Thursday after falling 5.06% on 19 November. Share prices around the world also rose on Thursday, even though the US announced new tariffs.
levels.why: Strong profits help firms to pay workers and invest, and calmer markets help savers.

levels.headline: China's factory profits jump 20.1% in October as exchanges make buying shares easier
levels.body:
The profits of big factories, mines and power firms in China were 20.1% higher in October than a year before. That is the fastest rise since May, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. The figures came out on Friday 27 November.
The same day, stock exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing said they will cut the minimum margin ratio, from 100% to 80%, from 30 November. This means people who borrow money to buy shares will need to put down less of their own money. It is meant to help markets after a big fall in shares linked to artificial intelligence.
Some shares have started to climb back. Japan's Nikkei rose 0.86% on Thursday.
levels.why: Strong factory profits and easier rules may help to calm worried investors.

levels.headline: Chinese factories made much bigger profits in October
levels.body:
The big factories, mines and power firms in China made 20.1% more profit in October than they did a year ago. It is the biggest rise since May. China's statistics office said so on Friday 27 November.
On the same day, the stock markets in three Chinese cities said they would change a rule. Investors can borrow money from a broker to buy shares. From 30 November, they will need to put down less of their own money. This is meant to help calm markets after a big fall in shares of companies linked to artificial intelligence.
Some shares have started to go back up. Japan's Nikkei index rose 0.86% on Thursday. Share prices around the world also rose on Thursday.
levels.why: China makes many of the goods we buy, so its factories matter to prices around the world.

levels.headline: China's factories earn much more money, and share markets get some help
levels.body:
Factories in China make things like toys, clothes and phones. In October, the big ones earned 20.1% more profit than a year before. That is the biggest rise since May. China's statistics office shared the news on Friday 27 November.
Share markets in Asia have been bumpy, especially for companies that work on artificial intelligence. Their prices fell a lot. To help, stock markets in three Chinese cities will change a rule from 30 November. People who borrow money to buy shares will not need to put down as much of their own money.
Share prices have started to go back up a little in Japan and Hong Kong.
levels.why: Good news from factories can help calm worried investors.

levels.headline: Chinese factories make a lot more money, and the stock markets get some help
levels.body:
China has many factories. They make things like toys, clothes and phones that people buy all around the world. In October, the big factories earned 20.1% more money than a year before. That is the biggest jump since May.
Share prices in Asia have been going up and down a lot. A share is a small piece of a company. Prices fell for companies that work on artificial intelligence. On 30 November, stock markets in three Chinese cities will make a rule easier. People who borrow money to buy shares will not need to put down as much of their own money.
Share prices in Japan and Hong Kong have started to climb back.
levels.why: Factories that do well can pay workers and keep making the things we buy.

levels.headline: Chinese factories made lots more money last month
levels.body:
China has lots of big factories. They make toys, clothes and phones that are sold all around the world. In October, they made 20.1% more profit than last year. Profit is the money a business keeps after it pays for everything.
Share prices in Asia have been jumping up and down. A share is a tiny piece of a company that people can buy. Some prices fell a lot. So some leaders in China are changing a rule to help. It will make buying shares a little easier.
Prices in places like Japan and Hong Kong have started to go back up. That is good news for people who own shares.
levels.why: If factories do well, it is good news for the workers there, and for shops that sell their goods.

levels.headline: Factories in China had a very good month
levels.body:
China has lots of big factories. They make toys, clothes and phones that children all over the world play with. In October, they earned a lot more money than last year. Making a profit means keeping some money after paying for everything.
Some people also own tiny pieces of companies, called shares. The prices of shares have been bouncing up and down, like a trampoline. So some leaders in China have made a rule a little easier. It should help the bouncing to calm down.
In some places, share prices have started to go back up again. That is nice news for the people who own them.
levels.why: Busy factories mean more jobs and more things to buy.
